Another special rule in diversity cases involves the judicial ban on fraudulent joinder, the situation when a plaintiff joins a nondiverse party in an
effort to block removal. Removal is permitted if plaintiff has no cause of action against the nondiverse defendant; the district court may sever the
nondiverse party from the action under Federal Rule 21. See Percy, Making a Federal Case of It: Removing Civil Cases to Federal Court Based on
Fraudulent Joinder, 91 Iowa L.Rev. 189 (2005). Some courts will remand the case to allow the diverse defendant to move for severance and then to
remove. See Osborn v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co., 341 F.Supp.2d 1123 (E.D.Cal. 2004). Which approach is preferable? See Marple, Removal to
Federal Court Based on Misjoinder of Parties, 41 Tex.Tech L.Rev. 551 (2009).
Relatedly, a plaintiff may try to block removal by joining a nondiverse state law claim with an unrelated federal claim. See 28 U.S.C. § 1441(c).
The current statute became effective in 2012. What is the constitutional significance of requiring the district court to sever and remand the claim that is
nonremovable? Removal also is permitted when a federal claim is joined with a claim that is nonremovable by statute (for example, an action under a
state worker’s compensation law). See 14B Wright, Miller & Steinman, Federal Practice and Procedure § 3722.3 (4th ed.).
(3)Removal Based on Diversity Jurisdiction— the Amount-in-Controversy
When jurisdiction is based on diversity jurisdiction, the case must meet the amount-in-controversy requirement. Explain whether the following
situations will affect removal on the basis of diversity jurisdiction:
(a)After removal, plaintiff amends the complaint to demand relief that is less than the amount-in-controversy requirement.
(b)The complaint seeks recovery for “no more than $75,000.”
(c)The complaint seeks declaratory relief.
(d)The complaint does not seek a sum certain for relief in a state that does not require an ad damnum clause.
In 2012, Congress amended the removal statute as it affects the jurisdictional amount. See 28 U.S.C. § 1446(c). The Supreme Court
interpreted this provision in DART CHEROKEE BASIN OPERATING CO. v. OWENS, 574 U.S. 81, 135 S.Ct. 547, 190 L.Ed.2d 495 (2014), a
case involving removal under the Class Action Fairness Act (CAFA), 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332(d) and 1453. The Court stated:
When a plaintiff invokes federal-court jurisdiction, the plaintiff’s amount-in-controversy allegation is accepted if made in good faith.* * *
